t: Indicators of Stress in Policymakers during Foreign Policy Crises
abs: Given the far-reaching consequences of decisions in foreign policy crises for a nation and the international arena, the quality of decision making in such situations needs careful attention. Case studies indicate that the quality of the performance of policymakers in crises is highly variable. Some policymakers reveal abilities and resourcefulness in crisis situations seldom seen in their day-to-day activities; whereas others appear erratic, devoid of sound judgment, and disconnected from reality. t: Eisenhower and Dulles: Who Made the Decisions?
abs: The overwhelming consensus among analysts of United States foreign policy during the Eisenhower administration is that it was dominated by Secretary of State John Foster Dulles. Regardless of their often differing assessments of the policies, these writers agree that Dulles' forceful personality, lengthy preparation, and keen intellect enabled him to control and even manipulate the congenial but bland and passive President Eisenhower. This conventional wisdom has been based on the public record, the period's journalistic accounts, and the appraisals of individuals who were largely outside the inner circles of both the White House and the State Department. Recently much primary source material has become available that calls into question this traditional interpretation of the Eisenhower-Dulles relationship. The Whitman File in the Eisenhower Library contains thousands of pages of transcripts of the president's daily phone conversations, minutes of formal and informal meetings, memoranda and other written communications, and Eisenhower's private diary. By using this new material in combination with the extant but often overlooked sources-Eisenhower's wartime papers, interviews with White House and State Department insiders available in both the Dulles Oral History Project and Columbia Oral History Collection, and studies of Eisenhower's pre-presidential career-the current scholar can determine that the standard view of Dwight Eisenhower on the leading strings of John Foster Dulles is highly problematic.

t: Traditionalizing Israeli Nationalism: The Development of Gush Emunim
abs: In the period following the 1973 Yom Kippur War, new has gainec increasing popular support in Israel. Called Gush Emunim (The Bloc of the Faithful), the presents an irredentist stance vis-a-vis the West Bank (Judea and Samaria) and other administered (the Sinai, the Gaza Strip, the Golan Heights). The focus of Gush's activities has been the establishment of Jewish settlements in these territories, beyond the Green Line. The settlements were founded with volunteered labor and without the consent of the (then-) Labour government.' The opponents of Gush viewed these settlements as illegal, blatant defiance of the government. Many critics demanded their removal, if necessary by force. Gush responded by rejecting the arguments. In their view each settlement was further move towards the integration of Eretz Yisrael, The Land of Israel, into Third Jewish commonwealth. Thus the leaders and supporters of Gush saw themselves standing party politics and, if necessary, above parliamentary process. They rejected the arguments of their opponents by claiming for their legitimacy based on (and not political) values. The ultimate value was that of Messianic Redemption. In this light the advent of the Jewish state was less the triumph of particular movement of national liberation, i.e., Zionism, than it was the beginnings of divinely inspired and ordained redemptive process. This process depends on, among other things, the territorial integrity of Eretz Yisrael.2 Failure to settle The Land or the withdrawal from presently occupied territories would be only secondarily military-political blunder. Such failure or withdrawal would constitute man's (or his government's) direct contravention of God's will: this would cause the interruption, or worse, the cessation, of the redemptive process. In the national election of May 17, 1977, control of the government was voted away from Labour and passed to the right-of-center Likud party headed by Menachem Begin. The new prime minister chose as the site for his first postelection speech the Gush settlement Kaddum. There he proclaimed Judea and Samaria to be a part of Israel. By July, the government announced plans for 16 new towns to be built on the West Bank. Seven were listed as projects planned by Gush Emunim. Two related transformations had occurred: political and religious legitimacy, hitherto disjointed, appeared to be conjoined in Likud government fostering Gush Emunim program. And Zionism, it was claimed, had undergone major and inevitable reorientation, finding at last its true expression. By examining the roots of the Gush Emunim movement, this paper seeks to illuminate these transformations. Of the varieties of political behavior the syndrome of hardball is especially intriguing to a spectator. In this syndrome, tough, ambitious, shrewdly calculating men vie for power and status behind a public veneer of civilization and idealistic concern (e.g., Machievelli, 1944; Caro, 1974; Bailey, 1969; Mayhew, 1974; Halperin, 1974; Bernstein & Woodward, 1974; Newhouse, 1973; O'Connor, 1975). The inside stories of what goes on behind the official public facade continually fascinate us, and the traditional journalistic exposes of such realities-always written with a tone of stylized shock and moral scandal-are guaranteed wide readership and are one of the enduring entertainments of the citizen and the professional observer of politics alike. My purpose is to sketch hardball as a subculture of the domestic and international political culture, a subculture constructed and sustained by a particular personality men with what is known clinically as a narcissistic personality disorder (Kohut, 1971, 1977).1 I will argue that such a model, which I will develop as an ideal type, potentially clarifies as a coherent syndrome various aspects of elite political behavior and partially explains the practices of the fascinating although often distasteful, objectionable, and sometimes gruesome political world we observe. The key internal feature of the narcissistic personality disorder politician (NP) is the simultaneous existence in the mind of two different and unintegrated subjective experiences of the self.2 In the foreground of the mind is a depleted, insecure self. Here is a sense of low self-esteem and of self-doubt, a strong propensity to feel inadequate, insecure, and ashamed, continuing worry about social acceptability, discomfort with intimacy, fear of genuineness, candor, and self-revelation, insecurity and apprehension about (vaguely defined) impending disaster. t: Birth Order and Paternal Namesake as Predictors of Affiliation with Predecessor by Presidents of the United States
abs: The 38 presidents of the United States were studied to test a report, based on a diverse sample of eminent men, that closer childhood affiliation of firstborn sons with their parents results in identification with authority in adulthood. Affiliation with the preceding president, defined as membership in the same political party, characterized seven of eight presidents who were the firstborn son and given the father's first name, but only one of nine presidents who was a later son with a brother given the father's first name. t: Political Psychology and the Proliferation of Interdisciplinary Fields in the Social-Behavioral Sciences: Part I
Toward an Adequate Explanation of the Politics of Working-Class Youth
abs: The assumptions and methodology of conventional political socialization research cannot capture the complexity of the relationship between social class position and the development of personal and political views. Standardized measures reflect the normative bias of the field, which assumes a single form of democratic citizenship; psychic deprivation theory, a recent explanatory model for political psychology, extends this bias into a rationale for viewing poor people as arrested in their psychological and political development. Our longitudinal research, exploring the meanings that 60 highability, working-class youths derive from their personal and political experience, finds different sources for their perceptions of themselves and of society. Their high personal optimism emerges from their view of themselves as hard-working individuals moving toward realistic goals; their political pessimism reflects their experiences with the lack of responsiveness of society to people in their socioeconomic position. This paper argues for broader definitions of democratic behavior that include the forms of participation and social concern that many of our interviewees evidence in their daily lives. We have been concerned these last six years with understanding and explaining the perceptions of self and society held by 60 white working-class youths from three very different communities near a northeast metropolis. These young people were interviewed first in 1972, when they were high-school seniors, and then again, four years later. Their fathers' occupations and their family incomes set these adolescents in the working class, and their own I.Q. scores and school records suggested that they would be upwardly mobile. Thus, their accounts of personal and political development place squarely before us the issue of the relationship between socioeconomic class, conceptions of self, and the development of political beliefs and actions. In our view, much work in political psychology explains social class differences and portrays working-class politics from a perspective that is seriously flawed. We do not share the conventional view of working-class citizens as authoritarian or incompletely socialized, constricted in their personal and political efficacy by psychological deprivation, projecting their insecurity and fear onto the social world. Instead, we find that working-class Americans, like everyone else, construct explanations of the social world and justifications for their own behavior that are based in the varieties of direct and indirect experience they have had with the way the world actually works; and that these interpretations of self-in-society are generated by the universal activity of finding and making meaning out of existence. The study of working-class politics must begin with the recognition that social stratification produces classes which differ both in their economic interests and in the particular meanings that individual members of these classes derive from their varying life experiences. t: On the Asking of Relevant Questions: Discussion Notes towards Understanding the Training of Political Psychologists
abs: Nothing is more appealing than the opportunity to pontificate, and no occasion is more inviting to the potential pontificator than the formation of a new organization devoted to such worthy ends as the pursuit of political psychology. Thus, the time for pontification seems uncomfortably right, as does the topic of this panel: the training of political psychologists. Indeed, on a subject as opaque as this one, pontification can almost pass itself off as reasoned argument. I hope my readers will be able to distinguish between the two in what follows. The status of advanced training in political psychology today may best be characterized as haphazard. I use this word advisedly, preferring it to a more evaluative characterization, such as or inadequate. The latter terms assume a knowledge on our part of what the training of the political psychologist ought to be, a knowledge we must uncover, rather than simply presume. As it happens, I believe that training in political psychology is inadequate as well as haphazard, and I will try to make a case for my evaluation later in this paper. I would add, parenthetically, that the reason for the haphazard quality of political psychology training is the deficient normative role of political psychology in the larger enterprise of political science.

t: Motives for Liberty, Equality, Fraternity: The Effects of Market and State
abs: Motives for liberty are identified as the need for personal causation, effectants, the control of one's own fate; motives for equality are a (small) part of the motive which also includes equity and need; motives for fraternity arise from the need for attachment expressed by friendship networks and community bonding. The market employs the need for fate control through individual effort; but democratic states through collective effort. The market employs the justice of equity; the democratic state the justice of need and sometimes the justice of parity. The market facilitates attachment through networks; the democratic state through community and family bonding. The good society, requires both market and democratic state to channel, reward, and fulfill these three motives. Analysis of these benign motives is the next step following the eighteenth-century transforThis is the story of three motives and two guardians of those motives: the market and the democratic state. It is an effort to illuminate the ways in which these two great allocative institutions shape human experience and so shape the human personality. It takes as the test of a society the quality of the human product rather than the size of the gross national product. It is about capitalism and socialism, but only insofar as capitalism relies relatively more on market transactions to govern who gets life's rewards and socialism relies relatively more on the authoritative allocation of values by agencies of the democratic state.
